title: The Day The Big Issue Launched With Five Vendors
dek: In September 1991 a magazine for homeless people to sell went on sale in London, and for a week almost nobody would sell it.

story.event: Launching a street magazine that homeless vendors buy and sell on, and surviving its first year
story.summary: Inspired by New York's Street News, Body Shop co-founder Gordon Roddick funded a feasibility study by his old friend John Bird, a former rough sleeper turned printer, and on 11 September 1991 they launched The Big Issue in London, a magazine homeless vendors buy cheaply and sell at a profit. Only five vendors came to the launch and almost none for a week afterwards; by June 1992 the magazine was losing £25,000 a month, and Roddick gave Bird three months to break even, which he did.
paragraphs: On 11 September 1991, outside St Martin-in-the-Fields on the corner of Trafalgar Square, John Bird and Gordon Roddick launched a magazine to be sold by homeless people. The television crews came; the vendors mostly did not. Bird had toured the places where people slept rough and been promised a crowd. Five turned up, and he later recalled having to dress them differently for different cameras.

The idea was Roddick's. In New York in 1990 the co-founder of The Body Shop had bought Street News from a homeless vendor and liked the scheme: sellers bought papers cheaply and sold them on. He turned to Bird, whom he had first met in Edinburgh in 1967, when Bird was 21 and sleeping rough. Bird had been homeless as a small child and had served time in prison; by 1991 he ran a printing business and, the magazine's own history says, did not want the job. Roddick paid him a daily rate for a feasibility study instead.

What Bird found was mixed. London's homeless organisations, he later said, asked why anyone would give homeless people the means to earn their own money. On the streets, most people told him to go away, but some said anything was better than begging. He came back convinced it would work, and the launch date left him about three months to gather a team and fill a first issue.

The rule that vendors pay for their copies was both the point and the trouble. Many rough sleepers were furious at being asked to buy what they sold, Bird said. For about a week after the launch, nobody came. Then a vendor called Ray Gray asked to buy another 50 papers and others followed; Bird recalled the count climbing from ten into the hundreds. His brother Peter, who ran distribution, said they won people over by turning up every day.

The money went fast. By June 1992, the magazine's history records, it was selling 150,000 copies and still losing £25,000 a month. Roddick gave Bird three months to break even or he would close it. "Incredibly, he managed it," Roddick said. Monthly at first, The Big Issue went weekly in 1993.

quote.text: When the person in authority makes more beneficial to the people the things from which they naturally derive benefit;-- is not this being beneficent without great expenditure? When he chooses the labours which are proper, and makes them labour on them, who will repine?
quote.source_title: The Analects of Confucius (from the Chinese Classics), tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #3330
quote.connection: Confucius held that if people are set to fitting work that builds on what already benefits them, nobody will complain. Bird and Roddick believed they had found such work, yet the first sellers protested and for a week none came. Whether that resistance meant the work was wrong, or only new, the story leaves open.

reflection: Most new things meet their first users looking smaller than planned: five people where you expected a crowd, a week with nobody, then one person asking for fifty more. What carried The Big Issue through that week was not a better speech but turning up at the same places each day until trust caught up.

If something you have offered has met suspicion, it may help to ask what the people you hoped to serve have been offered before, and how that went for them. Their caution is information rather than an insult, and it usually eases only with time and with you still being there.
invitation: Think of one person who has been slow to take up something you offered. Today, instead of explaining it again, ask them one question about what they have been offered before.

cross_checks.claim: The Big Issue was launched in London in September 1991 (on 11 September at St Martin-in-the-Fields)
Roddick got the idea from a Street News vendor in New York in 1990 and paid Bird for a feasibility study before Bird agreed to run it
Homeless people at first resisted having to buy the magazine to sell it, and vendors were hard to find in the first period
The magazine lost money for months and in 1992 Roddick threatened to stop funding it unless it turned round within three months
The Big Issue began as a monthly and became weekly in 1993

research_notes: Year of the New York encounter: The Big Issue's 25th-anniversary history, The Guardian (2020) and Bird at the DDN conference all say 1990; a 2010 student article (The Boar) says 1991. The story uses 1990. Bird's state in 1991: the 25th-anniversary history says he was married with two teenagers and had a printing business (his wife separated from him in 1992); a Cherwell interview has him saying he had virtually nothing and had just broken up with his first wife; DDN says his print business was struggling. The story says only that he ran a printing business and did not want the job. Study fee: The Guardian has Bird asking £200 a day and Roddick offering £100, without saying what was agreed, so the story says 'a daily rate'. Money: the 25th-anniversary history says The Body Shop invested £500,000 in the first three years; Wikipedia calls it £500,000 of start-up capital; the figure is not used in the story. The June 1992 figures (selling 150,000 copies, losing £25,000 a month) come only from the magazine's own history and are attributed to it; the history does not say whether 150,000 is per issue or cumulative, so the story repeats the wording without adding a unit. Roddick's deadline: Roddick (25th-anniversary history) says break even within three months or close; Bird (35th-anniversary piece) says no more money and three months to sort it out; The Guardian says only that Roddick was about to pull the plug. The story uses Roddick's version and his quotation. Rough-sleeper numbers in London in 1991 vary widely between sources (2,000 to 3,000; more than 6,000; Bird's 'about 10,000'), so none is used. The five-vendor launch and the Ray Gray episode rest on Bird's recollection in the 35th-anniversary piece, which draws on BBC Radio 4's The Reunion. The Guardian's own URL for 'How we made the Big Issue magazine' did not load; the Yahoo syndication is cited. Several detailed sources are the magazine's own publications and are marked as company archive. The Confucius passage concerns how a ruler should govern; it is applied by analogy.
